newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Azteca bares its teeth with IPO.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Azteca bares its teeth with IPO.

text.p: TV Azteca, which is going public today, has won a reputation as a scrappy fighter during its four-year rise from a flabby state-run television network to the pit bull of Mexico's media industry.

Privatized in 1993, the company and its billionaire owner Ricardo Salinas Pliego have emerged unscathed from a series of brawls with nearly everyone along the way: giant rival Grupo Televisa, the courts, politicians, even its own partners.

Despite the spats -- or maybe because of them -- Azteca capped a successful bid on Friday to float shares on the New York and Mexican bourses. It is expected to take in some $620 million for 22 percent of the company, though initial estimates after the pricing were for $526 million.
The stock was initially priced at $18.25 per ADS and 35.43 pesos per Mexican share.
"Azteca is the terrier of Mexican TV. They may get into a lot of scraps, but they usually come out on top," said a Mexico City media analyst who wished to remain anonymous.

At the helm of Azteca is Salinas Pliego, the controversial 41-year-old owner of the Elektra retail chain. The brash retail magnate used Elektra to help fund his bid for Azteca, a move which catapulted him to the number four spot on Mexico's list of wealthiest men, worth a reported $1.7 billion.

Salinas Pliego's hard-nosed business instincts helped Azteca take a bite out of Televisa, the former virtual monopoly that has lost a third of Mexico's audience and ad market share to Azteca in three years.

The new owners poured money into the company, building modern studios, pushing fast-paced U.S.-style news and talk-shows and undercutting Televisa's high ad rates. It also took aim at the media giant's successful soap operas that Televisa had peddled in Mexico and abroad for decades.

"You have to give Salinas Pliego credit for accomplishing a great deal in a short period of time. It caught the dinosaur (Televisa) asleep," said Niraj Gupta, a media analyst at Schroeder Wertheim in New York.
In becoming a strong rival to Televisa, Azteca also became a mouth-watering possibility as a public offering.
But Salinas Pliego's strong-arm tactics and admitted bad temper have also alientated several partners.

The public offering itself is due to a squabble between Salinas Pliego and the Saba family, minority partners who together with Salinas Pliego paid the lion's share of some $641 million for two state-owned channels in 1993.
Analysts say the Sabas were angered by Salinas Pliego's moves to increase his holdings in the company from 48 percent to 66 percent through buying stock options from creditor banks earlier this year.
Both sides had already bickered about programming and other daily decisions at the firm, analysts say.

To prevent the company from splitting, Salinas Pliego agreed to let the Sabas take profits on their investment by selling their stake to the public -- something Salinas Pliego said recently would not happen for a few years to come.

Azteca's IPO has angered U.S. network NBC, the subsidiary of General Electric that claims it has a right to 21.5 percent of Azteca under the terms of a 1994 joint venture that recently unravelled. NBC is suing Azteca for at least $132.5 million. Azteca, meanwhile, is fighting the law suit.
Salinas Pliego has also been dogged by reports of murky business ties.

His admitted dealings with the jailed brother of former President Carlos Salinas led to a congressional investigation last year to determine whether there was any foul play in the privatization. Salinas was president from 1988-1994.
The investigation was eventually scrapped, but an angry Salinas Pliego sued journalists who tried to cover the emerging scandal.
